interactions.label: Which of the following correctly describes C fibres compared with A-delta fibres

params.question: Which of the following correctly describes C fibres compared with A-delta fibres?

answers.text: Unmyelinated, conducting at under 2 m/s, carrying burning second pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. C fibres are unmyelinated and slow (under 2 m/s). They carry the burning, aching second pain that lingers after injury and account for roughly 80% of all nociceptive afferents.

answers.text: Thinly myelinated, conducting at up to 30 m/s, carrying sharp first pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes A-delta fibres, not C fibres. A-delta fibres are thinly myelinated, fast (up to 30 m/s), and carry the sharp, well-localised first pain felt immediately after a noxious stimulus.

answers.text: Unmyelinated, conducting at 15–20 m/s, carrying dull pressure sensation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: C fibres do conduct slowly, but at under 2 m/s — not 15–20 m/s. They carry burning second pain, not dull pressure. Intermediate velocities in that range do not characterise primary nociceptive afferents.

answers.text: Heavily myelinated, conducting at over 50 m/s, carrying thermal sensation only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Heavily myelinated, high-velocity fibres (A-beta) carry light touch and proprioception, not nociceptive signals. C fibres are unmyelinated and the slowest pain fibres, conducting at under 2 m/s.

overallFeedback.feedback: C fibres are unmyelinated and the slowest pain fibres (under 2 m/s), carrying burning second pain. The fast A-delta fibres (up to 30 m/s, thinly myelinated) carry the sharp, well-localised first pain.
Well done. C fibres are unmyelinated, slow, and carry burning second pain — the lingering ache that follows the sharp first pain transmitted by the faster A-delta fibres.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old boy is unable to communicate his pain verbally after an operation.

params.question: A 2-year-old boy is unable to communicate his pain verbally after an operation. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?

answers.text: FLACC scale, which scores facial expression, leg movement, activity, cry, and consolability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For children under four or patients who cannot speak, a behavioural scale is required. FLACC observes five observable domains without needing a verbal response, making it the validated choice here.
The NRS requires the patient to assign a number to their pain and is suited to most adults. A 2-year-old cannot use it reliably; a behavioural scale such as FLACC is the appropriate choice.
The DN4 is a validated screening tool for neuropathic pain in adults who can answer questions about pain quality verbally. It is not designed for pre-verbal children.
NIPS is the validated tool specifically for neonates. For a pre-verbal toddler beyond the neonatal period, FLACC is the correct behavioural scale.

overallFeedback.feedback: For a pre-verbal 2-year-old, a behavioural scale is needed. FLACC scores five observable behaviours — facial expression, leg movement, activity, cry, and consolability — without requiring the child to speak.
Correct. FLACC is the validated behavioural scale for pre-verbal children beyond the neonatal period — it scores observable responses rather than self-report.

interactions.label: All common opioid side effects — including sedation, nausea, and constipation —

params.question: All common opioid side effects — including sedation, nausea, and constipation — typically resolve within days as tolerance develops.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Opioid-induced constipation is unique: tolerance does not develop to this effect. Sedation and nausea typically ease within days, but constipation persists throughout treatment. Every patient starting regular opioids needs a stimulant laxative prescribed from day one.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Sedation and nausea usually resolve as tolerance develops, but constipation does not undergo tolerance. A stimulant laxative such as senna must be started from day one and continued throughout opioid treatment; a bulk-forming laxative alone is not sufficient.

interactions.label: A patient with advanced cancer is on oral morphine 30 mg daily and uses five bre

params.question: A patient with advanced cancer is on oral morphine 30 mg daily and uses five breakthrough doses over the past 24 hours. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Increase the total daily morphine dose by 30–50% and reassess within 24–48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Using more than two to three breakthrough doses per day indicates the background dose is too low. Increasing the total daily dose by 30–50% and reassessing is the standard titration protocol. There is no ceiling dose for cancer pain.

answers.text: Add a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug before increasing the opioid dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An NSAID may be appropriate for inflammatory or bone pain, but the priority here is correcting inadequate background analgesia. Five breakthrough doses in 24 hours is a clear signal to increase the total daily morphine dose by 30–50%.

answers.text: Continue the current dose as five breakthrough doses are within acceptable limits for the first week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The threshold is two to three breakthrough doses per day. Five doses indicates the background dose is insufficient. Waiting risks prolonged uncontrolled pain; the dose should be increased by 30–50% immediately.

answers.text: Switch to a transdermal fentanyl patch because oral morphine carries a ceiling dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral morphine has no ceiling dose in cancer pain. Transdermal fentanyl is an alternative when the oral route fails — not when the dose simply needs adjustment. The correct action is to increase the background oral dose by 30–50%.

overallFeedback.feedback: Five breakthrough doses in 24 hours means the background dose is too low. Increase the total daily morphine dose by 30–50% and reassess. Oral morphine carries no ceiling dose for cancer pain.
Correct. More than two to three breakthrough doses per day signals inadequate background analgesia — increase the total daily dose by 30–50% and reassess in 24–48 hours.

interactions.label: A terminally ill patient becomes unable to swallow overnight and develops restle

params.question: A terminally ill patient becomes unable to swallow overnight and develops restlessness and noisy respiratory secretions. Which set of drugs should ideally have been prescribed in advance?

answers.text: Morphine, midazolam, haloperidol, hyoscine butylbromide, and an antiemetic — all as subcutaneous prescriptions written before the crisis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Anticipatory prescribing means these five subcutaneous drugs are written before the crisis, not during it. Morphine relieves breathlessness, midazolam manages restlessness, haloperidol treats delirium, hyoscine butylbromide reduces secretions, and an antiemetic addresses nausea.

answers.text: Continue oral morphine, oral diazepam, and oral metoclopramide as the patient was tolerating them previously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Once swallowing stops, the oral route is no longer feasible. In the active dying phase, all medications must be given subcutaneously. Anticipatory prescribing prepares this transition in advance so there is no delay when symptoms arise.

answers.text: Intravenous lorazepam and intravenous haloperidol, titrated in a critical care setting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The subcutaneous route — not intravenous — is the gold standard in palliative care for comfort and ease of administration outside hospital. Transfer to critical care is not appropriate for a patient on an end-of-life pathway.

answers.text: Oral dexamethasone and nebulised saline, with subcutaneous morphine held until breathing deteriorates further

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting until breathing deteriorates further means prescribing under pressure and risks delayed treatment. Anticipatory prescribing means morphine and all four other drugs are written in advance so they can be given immediately when needed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Anticipatory prescribing means writing five subcutaneous prescriptions before symptoms arise: morphine (dyspnoea), midazolam (restlessness), haloperidol (delirium), hyoscine butylbromide (secretions), and an antiemetic — prescribed in advance, not during the emergency.
Correct. Anticipatory prescribing writes five subcutaneous drugs before any crisis: morphine, midazolam, haloperidol, hyoscine butylbromide, and an antiemetic.
